title: Smith v. Northeast Presbytery
disposition_detail: The complaint was sustained: the June 8 complaint against Presbytery’s May action was timely and in order; BCO 11-4 did not prohibit care for members of a dissolved congregation, though it did not itself require such care; and Presbytery remained responsible for pastoral care in these circumstances. The matter was remanded to Presbytery for adjudication.
first_summary: Smith challenged Northeast Presbytery’s ruling that his complaint was untimely and unconstitutional after Presbytery dissolved Grace Church and postponed a proposed Braintree mission. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding it timely because the May action first indicated that former members were outside the PCA. BCO 11-4 did not bar Presbytery from caring for them, and Presbytery’s April referral to its missions committee left it responsible for pastoral care. The matter was remanded for adjudication.
summary: Smith challenged Northeast Presbytery’s ruling that his complaint was untimely and unconstitutional after it dissolved Grace Church and indefinitely postponed a proposed Braintree mission. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded it for Presbytery adjudication. The May action first revealed Presbytery’s view that former members were outside the PCA, so the June complaint was timely. BCO 11-4 neither barred nor itself required care; responsibility arose here from the April referral to Presbytery’s missions committee. Care need not take the form of a mission, and mere dissolution alone would not create that responsibility.

sources.supports: Complaint, issues, adopted judgment, reasoning, qualifications, and remand.
Unanimous SJC approval and express warning that the later reproduced panel judgment was not affirmed.

evidence_notes.identity_and_adoption: The caption identifies Judicial Case 92-1, Smith v. Northeast Presbytery; the SJC unanimously approved its decision (lines 1–3, 9, 102; printed p. 198).
evidence_notes.dispute: Smith complained of Presbytery’s failure to care for former Grace Church members; Presbytery ruled the complaint untimely and constitutionally defective (lines 36–50; printed p. 195).
evidence_notes.outcomes_and_reasons: The SJC found the complaint timely, held BCO 11-4 did not prohibit care, found a pastoral-care responsibility, and sent the matter back for adjudication (lines 52–65, 70–89; printed pp. 195–197).
evidence_notes.qualifications: A mission church was not the only permissible care; mere dissolution alone would create no responsibility. Here the April referral reasonably promised continuing care until further action, withdrawal, or transfer (lines 89–100; printed pp. 197–198).
evidence_notes.incorporated_decisions: The SJC concurred with a quoted 1988 constitutional-inquiry answer about membership rolls but distinguished the unresolved duty of pastoral care. The reproduced panel judgment was expressly not affirmed (lines 93–100, 109–123; printed pp. 198–199).

source_limits: The synopsis relies solely on the supplied SJC record. The separately reproduced panel judgment is not treated as operative.

score_reasons.concrete_dispute: Identifies the challenged out-of-order ruling and failure to provide pastoral care.
score_reasons.decision: States the favorable rulings, qualification concerning BCO 11-4, and remand.
score_reasons.decisive_reason: Explains why the May action made the complaint timely and why the April referral continued responsibility.
score_reasons.distinctive_value: Preserves the distinctions between permission and obligation, mission status and other care, and referral versus mere dissolution.
score_reasons.fidelity: Separates the adopted SJC judgment from the unaffirmed panel judgment and preserves stated qualifications.
score_reasons.economy: Retains only facts needed to explain timeliness, responsibility, and relief.

verification_notes: Rechecked the operative SJC judgment and reasoning against the later panel text. The final summary clarifies that BCO 11-4 did not itself require care, that responsibility arose from the April referral, that care could take forms other than a mission, and that mere dissolution alone would not suffice.
